title: IBM just placed two very different tech bets in one day
excerpt: Two partnerships. Two industries. One company quietly expanding its reach in ways investors should notice.
content_html:
A hundred years ago, International Business Machines Corporation (IBM) built machines that helped the United States count its census.

On September 10, 2026, it did something stranger. It opened a quantum computing lab tied to Swiss defense spending, then released an open-source AI model built to map the moon.

Most companies pick one narrative and repeat it until investors believe it. IBM picked two, on the same day, with two entirely different partners: a defense contractor and a space agency.

A Swiss quantum lab taps IBM's newest asset

The quantum hub is not really a research story. It is a fighter jet story. Switzerland's offset agreement with Lockheed Martin Corporation (LMT) traces back to a 2021 order for 36 F-35A jets, a deal worth $9.1 billion.

That purchase created a Lockheed Martin offset obligation worth about $3 billion, or 60% of the contract's value, according to armasuisse figures reported by The Defense Watch.

Most of that obligation has gone toward manufacturing work such as engine training systems, canopy components and ammunition production.

A quantum lab at ETH Zurich is a different kind of payback. It will host Switzerland's first IBM Quantum System Two by the end of 2026, according to IBM's newsroom. The shift toward advanced technology, rather than factory work, comes as the F-35 deal faces political pressure over cost overruns and U.S. tariffs, according to DefenseMirror.

IBM, not Lockheed, actually supplies and operates that machine. Lockheed gets credit toward a binding obligation tied to jets it already sold. IBM gets a government-funded showcase for its hardware, arriving through a defense contractor's political obligation rather than a commercial sale IBM would have had to win outright.

The timing sharpens that read. IBM completed its acquisition of HRL Laboratories in late August, according to a company release, adding in-house expertise in quantum sensing.

Quantum sensing for navigation is one of two joint research areas named for the hub, according to IBM's newsroom. That is exactly the capability IBM just bought. IBM is not licensing hardware to a defense partner. It is running technology it acquired three weeks earlier, inside a deal structured to satisfy someone else's political obligation.

NASA and IBM open-source a lunar AI model

Hours after the Zurich announcement, IBM and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) released the NASA IBM Lunar Foundation Model, according to IBM's newsroom.

The model is trained on decades of lunar observation data and made freely available. Reuters covered the release, noting it is meant to help identify ice, craters and other lunar surface features.
